questions.question: Explain why the state intervenes in markets and describe the four instrument families with examples.
questions.expected_answer: Intervention answers market outcomes society won't accept: essentials priced beyond the poor, uncharged externalities, overconsumed harmful goods, underconsumed merit goods, and brutal for-whom answers under unequal incomes. Families: indirect taxes (VAT, excise/sin taxes, fuel levy) — raising revenue and discouraging consumption; subsidies (public transport, agricultural support) — the state paying part of the cost to cheapen the good; welfare (grants, public healthcare, no-fee schools) — bypassing prices entirely with direct provision and transfers; and price controls — maximum prices, minimum prices and the minimum wage — legislating the price itself.

questions.question: Trace an indirect tax and a subsidy through the market diagram, including the burden split and one honest cost of each.
questions.expected_answer: A tax is a per-unit cost to sellers: supply shifts leftward, giving a higher equilibrium price and lower quantity; the price typically rises by less than the full tax, so the burden splits between buyers and sellers. A subsidy mirrors it: supply shifts rightward — lower price, higher quantity (cheaper bus fares, more riders). Honest costs: a tax set too high breeds smuggling and illicit trade; a subsidy must be funded by taxation elsewhere (opportunity cost) and can be captured by producers as fatter margins instead of lower prices. Both instruments SHIFT the supply curve — they don't merely relabel the price.

questions.question: Compare the ceiling and the floor — placement, consequence, and secondary effects — and give the balanced minimum wage argument.
questions.expected_answer: A binding maximum price sits BELOW equilibrium: quantity demanded exceeds supplied — a permanent shortage rationed by queues, favourites and limits, leaking into black-market sales above the ceiling, with quality often slipping. A binding minimum price sits ABOVE equilibrium: supplied exceeds demanded — a surplus the state must buy, store or export, at budget cost. The minimum wage is a labour-market floor: mechanically it predicts a labour surplus (unemployment pressure); the case for cites dignity, reduced working poverty and wages respent into the circular flow; the case against cites priced-out young and unskilled workers and informalisation. The honest verdict: a trade-off whose size is empirical.
